Parliament questions and answers

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Parliament is like a different world - even with its own language - but we have an expert who can decrypt governments responses to important questions which usually fly under the radar.

Unique Selling Point:
the parliamentary q and a's they are hilariously sad. So I met this woman Renee Thompson who has worked in government and now has the Thompson trust - she monitors parliament and all their bs... she can convert government speak into understandable relatable english - with her own twist! Here are some great ones she has picked out just on one department but we can do several departments:

Questions and answers on public service and administration...DPSA (all national gov employees)
The number of employees that have been doing business with the state - nearly 500 employees. This is not allowed...

Employees who took leave during january this year for i). "family responsibly"( if your child is sick, if someone dies, or a family is ill - and its only 5 days a year) 13,307 employees ii). sick leave (full pay) 48,576!!!! - Renee says: "yeah right" haha iii) Took Special leave - renee: "this is suspended people" - 13,518...

On the public wage bill: it currently costs us R628 billion!!! and they want to decrease by R37.8 billion (very current because unions are threatening to strike)... so how are gov planning on doing this... they says they are not employing anymore ppl but are advertising more posts!??! They say they need to minimize spending on "litigations against the state, office accommodation, corruption, and fraud, use of consultants, irregular expenditure..." Renee - so in other words they are doing nothing.

On some of the frivolous things the government pays employees for: Leave that has rolled over - so the government will pay you back money if you dont take your leave... (Renee says often the trick is that employee don't fill out leave forms!) - you have 21 days per year and for employees longer than 15 years you get 30 days - so gov paid employees R7.3 million at national, and R65 million at provincial gov. Renee says: "we're spending money like its endless"

What number of Public Service employees are PERCAUTIONARY suspended on full pay and how much that cost us?
National department 29. (average is 2 months - to a year - HOW IS THAT AN AVERAGE?!)
2017/2018 is R 73 976, 00
2018/2019 is R 1 319 887, 00
2019/2020 is R 26 183 216, 00
** SOME OF THE PPL ARE NAMED and they are suspended for fraud...for example higher education and training R1.3 million for one employee... assistant director at TVET college manipulation of data - over a million. There are cases of sexual assault....
Renee says: "ppl come back from suspension with degrees...."

People on suspension for : Misconduct - someone in the free state premiere's office for theft fraud and bribery - over a million! Another is public works and infrastructure for more than a year - another million - lockdown is the reason given... then there are ppl who were "drunk on duty"...
What qualifications are needed for senior manager (SMS) if they have the necessary qualifications? A degree and a certain amount of exp...post grad and 10 years gov experience... "there are currently 201 DDG posts in National government of which 135 are filled and 66 are vacant. Prior to 1 April 2015 there was no prescription on the educational requirements." Renee says matriculants who is connected waltz in and earn more than you... (an example is the DG of Public service and administration... she's a young female -she was suspended and used that period to study - did a Masters degree - and then because she's member of the ANC in Gauteng - she became HOD in one of the security clusters...)




Summary:
So we would interview the head of the DPSA who says they are saving money and give them examples from their own answers. Then we'd interview renee with a presenter and have sexy responses (like Redisa story), then we would interview someone in Public finance or treasury to get perspective... so we are translating government speak for our audience and decoding their cryptic nonsense

Further information:
Potentially we would pay Kate a producer fee to assist me in writing a funny script... cos this will all be in the script

Press Release:


Parliamentary Q&A

The role of Parliament in manifesting the democracy South Africans treasure, cannot be underestimated. The members of the house elected to represent ordinary people are meant to be their voice. Parliament is accountable to the people – and every word uttered there matters. Or it should – but Carte Blanche discovers it takes an expert to decipher the often-obscure answers to oversight questions posed at the heart of democratic process.

Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


V/O: Parliament – derived from the French word parler – to talk. The home of our legislative body and a major source of hot air released by our politicians.

EFF: drama….

V/O: Then there’s the Speaker – who doesn’t always let everyone else speak.

NATS SOUND

Baleka: Honourable member…….blah blah.

V/O: But sometimes she does.

NATS SOUND

Zuma: Nkandla…..Laughing is not hurtful, it’s healthy. Hee hee.

V/O: But all this jocular jabber can be rather tiring… SYS_SYNC_0313_00101_BRAHMS_LULLABY_Martin_Nicholas_Gratton

Video: Sleeping MP

V/O: One of parliament most important functions is the oversight of government. MPs can question any Minister of any Department in the Parliamentary Q&A sessions. But just because you ask a straight question, doesn’t mean you’ll get a straight answer.


Ralph: The problem is that no one gets punished for providing mediocre answers.

V/O: Former government employee turned political analyst Ralph Mothekga believes the so-called answers are designed to bamboozle public opinion.


Ralph: There are no consequences for coming across as caring less about answering this question diligently.

Link: From big name accounting firms to huge construction companies to leading public relations organizations, South Africa’s produced some world class spin doctors. But it’s in all spheres of government that the delicate art of spin has been taken to a new level.

V/O: Renee Thompson is a 20-year veteran well-versed in parliamentary speak.


Derek: Do these sessions help to keep politicians honest in any way?

Renee: If you answer incorrectly then you lying to parliament. So when a Minister signs off on an answer it has to be the truth.

V/O: But with most of us struggling to pay attention in our own Zoom meetings, who is actually watching the Parliamentary Q&A sessions, let alone reading the written answers?



Derek: 00:07:26:03 - 00:07:30:21

Who takes any of these answers seriously and actually analyzes them?

00:07:31:05 - 00:08:02:24

Renee: Well, the members of parliament are supposed to. I feel maybe that that's always lacking where you just submit a question, the answer’s complex and then nothing, or there's no follow up.

00:08:33

Renee: And and I mean, the opposition parties and the departments should take responsibility for that.

Link: Parliament is a different world. It has its own campus, its own protocols and it seems that government also has its own terminology to try and baffle the public when it comes to answering those difficult questions.

V/O: And so Carte Blanche delved into some parliamentary responses from the Department of Public Service and Administration or DPSA. Here’s the spin from Minister Senzo Mchunu.



Minister: In practice the majority of government employees are hardworking. They are honest. They are dedicated.

V/O: But what the Honourable Minister fails to mention is what the vast minority get up to.


Mrs Q: And they will try and be as vague as possible. You try and answer without answering.

V/O: Former state employee turned whistle-blower, Mrs Q, is fluent in spin. We asked her to interpret the DPSA’s parliamentary responses. And if you’re

wondering what the DPSA does, it’s like one big HR department for all 2.1 million government officials.


QUESTIONS: STATE EMPLOYEES DOING BUSINESS WITH THE STATE


D: 437. It's almost like an admission of guilt, by doing business with the state?

It’s a conflict of interest means which you are not allowed to do. And every senior civil servant is supposed to fill out a declaration. At the end of February 2021, it was four hundred and eighty two..

ONLY 8 out of these were given official permission, 37 have disciplinary hearings, and only 12 have police cases. Coincidentally at the same time, another question to Eskom shows that nearly 5,500 of its employees have failed to fill out their declaration forms.

MRS Q: Meaning that they are potentially still doing business with the state and at an entity that is bankrupt.

The identified Eskom employees have since been referred for disciplinary’s.

Derek: Question number 454 relating to the reduction of the public sector wage bill?

Mrs Q: The minister of finance has repeatedly said that the public wage bill must be reduced and there would be no increases. And yet there are increases now.

The public wage bill is a large chunk of our national budget’s R2 Trillion spend allowance. A staggering R629 billion. This is how much our roughly 2million civil servants cost us.

R: We pay more for the public service but the quality of the services keeps on declining. Who cuts the public sector wage bill shortly before the election? The problem is double talk.

Question number 232, the average length of time that it's been on suspension?

Mrs Q: Yeah, this is actually just paid leave. and you would even get your increase while you are on suspension.

I mean, the amount that has been spent on suspensions in 2017-2018 financial year is R73000, and now 26 million!

Two officials in the Eastern Cape’s department of sport, recreation, arts and culture, were suspended for 281 days for failure to comply with procurement procedures. They’ve still received their combined salaries of over R2.5 million and the case has continued because of interference with the investigation.

Mrs Q: You cannot steal without the guys in the procurement department working with you,

D: SAY THAT AGAIN?

Mrs Q: It's a team effort, because it cannot only be one person. You get you three quotes, And even if you get cheap, you’ll say, but okay, add another zero.

In the Freestate’s Office of the premier an employee who has been suspension for a year for theft, fraud and bribery, has been paid over a R1 million.

Q: You get to chill at home, maybe work on your Tick-Tock skills...The sad thing is, is that people come back after the suspension and just move get moved to another department. or get a slap on the wrist.

Let's get a question 309. Employees whove been or are currently absent from work, but it's still receiving their full salaries. This was stage three of lockdown?

Q : And during the December holiday, You can be very creative with leave forms. There were over thirteen thousand public servants on family responsibility leave, which coincided with Christmas and New Year.

D: So what are we saying here? that 322,000 employees just took time off?

QThey took a break. And sick full pay - R48,000…

D: 48,000. That’s a long hangover.

you’re stealing time from government.

Over and above the time stolen, employees are also paid out for the days they don’t take - over the past two years this was R135 million.

I mean, sick leave, it's one of those leaves that actually you see people abusing.

The DPSA has declined an interview, and despite their parliamentary answers airing in this program, they haven’t responded to our further questions.

We've made light of a lot of these answers, but truly it’s sad?

And the Department of Public Service and Administration is responsible for all civil servants. It is during a time where government cannot afford to be wasting money.

Renee Thompson:

00:10:41:13 - 00:10:57:27

really. Yeah. I mean, it's when you look at it, I actually find it shocking that not more people take notice of it because it happens every week that responses come back. So

V/O: The last word on parliamentary Q&A comes from that legendary politician Winston Churchill:

“The question we must ask ourselves is not whether we like or do not like what is going on, but what we are going to do about it.”
